meta.audience: Readers of the small plates, and the Lamanites specifically
meta.date: ~420–361 BC (238 years after Lehi left Jerusalem)

world_behind.title: Addressed to the enemy
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says these things are written "for the intent of the benefit of our brethren the Lamanites." Enos had secured a covenant that the record would reach them; one generation later the stated readership has changed accordingly. Jarom is writing for people whose armies are attacking his cities in verse 7.

world_behind.title: He declines to write his own revelations
world_behind.text: Verse 2 says he will not write his prophesying or his revelations because his fathers already revealed the plan of salvation. No other writer in the record refuses on that ground. The book is short by decision.

world_behind.title: "The plan of salvation" arrives as a known phrase
world_behind.text: The phrase enters the record here and appears only twice more, both in Alma. Jarom uses it as a thing his readers will recognize, which suggests the framework was in place two centuries after the landing and did not need explaining.

world_behind.title: The record's only sabbath
world_behind.text: Verse 5 says they kept the sabbath day holy. It is the sole explicit statement in the whole book that this people observed it, in a record that repeatedly says they kept the law of Moses. The observance is mentioned once and never discussed.

world_behind.title: An inventory of a manufacturing economy
world_behind.text: Verse 8 lists gold, silver, fine wood, buildings, machinery, iron, copper, brass, and steel, plus tools and a named weapons set: arrow, quiver, dart, javelin. "Machinery" occurs nowhere else in scripture. Two hundred years after arriving with tents, the description is of a people who manufacture.

world_behind.title: The answer to Sherem, institutionalized
world_behind.text: Verse 11 says the teachers taught the law of Moses "and the intent for which it was given," persuading the people to look forward to the Messiah. That is exactly the position Sherem attacked one book earlier, and here it is standing policy rather than one prophet's argument.

words.text: A written descent line, and in the Hebrew Bible it is what establishes a claim to land, to priesthood, or to a throne. Jarom gives it as his whole reason for writing and then supplies none. What he passes on instead is the object itself, so what gets tracked is custody.

A light spear made for throwing, shorter than the javelin listed next to it. The verse does not say weapons and leave it there. It names them one at a time: "yea, the sharp pointed arrow, and the quiver, and the dart, and the javelin" (v. 8). That is how an armory gets written down, not how a war gets described. The word appears nowhere else in this record, and the King James Bible puts it in a list of the weapons that cannot hurt leviathan.

cites.quote: yea, the sharp pointed arrow, and the quiver, and the dart, and the javelin

spans.text: yea, the sharp pointed arrow, and the quiver, and the dart, and the javelin

words.text: Shown to be true by event. The verb turns a promise into a finding. Jarom is not quoting the prosperity clause as encouragement; he is reporting that two centuries of history have tested it, and the sentence reads like a note in a ledger.

The prophets are the ones doing it. Jarom writes that they "did threaten the people of Nephi, according to the word of God" (v. 10), and the content of the threat is given in the same sentence: keep the commandments or be destroyed off the face of the land. This form of the word appears once in the King James Bible, when the council orders the apostles to stop preaching. There it is what authority does to silence men. Here it belongs to the prophets, and what they threaten with is the covenant's own terms.

cites.quote: did threaten the people of Nephi, according to the word of God

spans.text: did threaten the people of Nephi, according to the word of God

words.text: Patience under provocation, sustained over time. It is attached to the teachers rather than to God, and the object of the patience is the congregation. In a chapter that describes a people as hard-hearted, deaf, blind, and stiff-necked, this is the word for what the prophets did about it.

Cut into metal rather than written on it. Jarom has just said again that his own plates are small, and then sends his readers to the other plates, where "the records of our wars are engraven" (v. 14). The word keeps the physical fact in view: every line has to be cut, and length costs labor. The King James Bible has it once, of the law cut into stones. Here it is the ordinary term for how this people keeps history.

cites.quote: the records of our wars are engraven

spans.text: the records of our wars are engraven

phrases.term: For what could I write more than my fathers have written?
phrases.text: A rhetorical question that functions as an editorial policy. Jarom answers it himself. Nothing. Then he stops. It is the only place in the record where a keeper of the plates declines to add on the grounds that the subject is covered, and it is offered without apology.

phrases.term: The hardness of their hearts, and the deafness of their ears, and the blindness of their minds, and the stiffness of their necks
phrases.text: Four faculties, four failures, in a single clause. Heart, ears, mind, neck. The list is Isaiah's diagnostic vocabulary compressed into one sentence, and Jarom uses it as a standing description of the people he is about to call prosperous.

phrases.term: Has not as yet swept them off from the face of the land
phrases.text: The same verb turns up four verses later for what the Nephites do to the Lamanites in battle. Judgment and warfare share a word here, and the "as yet" is doing the work. The sentence treats destruction as deferred rather than avoided.

phrases.term: As many as are not stiffnecked and have faith, have communion with the Holy Spirit
phrases.text: "Communion" is Paul's word for sharing in something, the cup or the fellowship of the Spirit, and this is its only appearance in the record. It names a participation, a quieter claim than the visions Jarom has just declined to write down. The condition attached is stated negatively: the un-stiffnecked already share in it. Access is ordinary, and the limiting factor is a posture rather than a calling.

phrases.term: They observed to keep the law of Moses and the sabbath day holy
phrases.text: The record's single sabbath sentence, placed inside a list of civic virtues: they profaned not, they did not blaspheme, the laws were strict. Religion is being described here as public order, which is the sort of description a settled colony would produce.

phrases.term: In fine workmanship of wood, in buildings, and in machinery
phrases.text: The most specific description of Nephite material culture in the small plates, and "machinery" is unique to it. Nothing is said about what the machinery did. The verse moves straight from it to iron and copper and then to weapons, and the list's momentum is the point.

phrases.term: Inasmuch as ye will keep my commandments ye shall prosper in the land
phrases.text: The promise given to Lehi, quoted by Nephi twice, and here declared verified. Jarom is the first writer to check it against a long run of history, and the verdict is recorded in a subordinate clause.

phrases.term: Teaching the law of Moses, and the intent for which it was given
phrases.text: Two objects for one verb, and the second is the controversial one. Sherem had accused Jacob of converting the law into worship of a future being; this verse makes the same practice the ordinary curriculum. The record does not note the connection.

phrases.term: Believe in him to come as though he already was
phrases.text: The sharpest statement of forward-looking faith in the record, and it occurs once. Not believe that he will come, but believe in him as present. The teaching method described is to collapse the tense, and verse 12 reports that it worked.

phrases.term: They did prick their hearts with the word, continually stirring them up unto repentance
phrases.text: The verb is Peter's at Pentecost, where the crowd is "pricked in their heart" and asks what to do. Here it is a maintained condition, continual and running over generations, and it is credited with keeping the nation alive.

verses.label: v. 1–2
verses.title: The terms, and a refusal
verses.text: Write for the genealogy; the plates are small; the audience is the Lamanites; and then the decision not to record his own prophesying or revelations because the fathers have covered it. Two verses, and one of them is an argument for brevity.

verses.label: v. 3–4
verses.title: The people, twice
verses.text: Hard, deaf, blind, and stiff-necked. Then, immediately, many among them have revelations and are not all stiffnecked. Jarom gives the harsh assessment first and the qualification second, and the qualification is what carries the condition for communion with the Spirit.

verses.label: v. 5–6
verses.title: Two hundred years, both sides
verses.text: Nephites strong, law and sabbath kept, no profanity or blasphemy, strict laws. Lamanites scattered, more numerous, given to murder and to drinking the blood of beasts. The contrast is drawn without transition and the second half is written by an enemy.

verses.label: v. 7–9
verses.title: War, wealth, and a verdict
verses.text: Repeated attacks repelled by kings and leaders who were mighty in faith and taught the people; fortified cities; then the metals, the buildings, the machinery, and the weapons; and then the reason given for all of it, which is that the promise was verified. Prosperity is presented as evidence.

verses.label: v. 10–12
verses.title: How it was held together
verses.text: Prophets threatened destruction; priests and teachers labored with long-suffering, teaching the law and its intent and persuading the people to believe in a Messiah as though present; and by so doing they were kept from being destroyed. The nation's survival is credited to sustained teaching.

verses.label: v. 13–15
verses.title: The close
verses.text: Two hundred thirty-eight years, most of them spent in wars, contentions, and dissensions; the plates are small; the wars are on the other record; and the plates go to Omni. Three verses, and the middle one is a redirection to a book the reader does not have.

chapter.title: The shortest justification for brevity in the record
chapter.text: Jarom asks what he could write beyond what his fathers wrote, answers nothing, and means it. Every other keeper complains about space; he cites sufficiency. The book that results is fifteen verses and covers roughly sixty years.

chapter.title: The prosperity promise gets audited
chapter.text: Verse 9 reports the word "verified" after two centuries. This is the record doing something it rarely does. It tests an earlier prediction against elapsed time and writes down the result, and the finding is recorded in passing.

chapter.title: Survival is credited to teaching
chapter.text: Verse 7 has fortified cities and mighty leaders; verse 12 says what actually kept them from destruction was prophets pricking hearts with the word, continually. The chapter reports the military success and then quietly assigns the credit elsewhere.

chapter.title: The law is taught with its purpose attached
chapter.text: What Sherem called perversion is here the standing curriculum: the law of Moses and the intent for which it was given, with the Messiah believed in as though already present. One book after the controversy, it is settled practice and nobody argues.

chapter.title: The people are described in contradictory terms and both are left standing
chapter.text: Verse 3 calls them hard, deaf, blind, and stiff-necked; verse 4 says many have revelations; verse 5 says they keep the law and the sabbath and do not blaspheme. Jarom does not resolve it. A population is being described.

chapter.title: The book's stated purpose is the one thing it does not do
chapter.text: Written so the genealogy may be kept, it records no genealogy. The plates pass from Enos to Jarom to Omni, and that succession appears to be what "genealogy" meant here, a line of custody.

applications.title: Know when you have nothing to add
applications.text: Jarom stopped because the subject was covered. Before writing or speaking at length, ask honestly whether you are adding something or restating what is already available.

applications.title: Check the promise against your own history
applications.text: Jarom looked back over two hundred years and reported a finding. Take a promise you were given and audit it against what has actually happened, and write down the result either way.

applications.title: Teach the reason with the rule
applications.text: Whenever you pass on a practice to a child, a class, or a new colleague, give the intent for which it was given alongside it. The chapter treats the second half as the part that changes behavior.

applications.title: Believe as though already
applications.text: The method described is to live toward something future as if it were present. Pick one promise you are waiting on and act this week as though it had arrived.

applications.title: Keep pricking, continually
applications.text: The result in this chapter came from sustained repetition. In whatever you are trying to hold together, the chapter's model is frequency.

applications.title: Notice who gets the credit
applications.text: The walls held, but the chapter says the teaching is what saved them. Look at something that went well for you and ask what actually did the work.

questions.text: What do I keep saying that has already been said better, and what would silence make room for?
Which of the four is most true of me right now: hard heart, deaf ears, blind mind, or stiff neck?
Is my access to the Spirit limited by calling or by posture, and which do I usually blame?
If I audited the promises I have been given against my actual history, what would the ledger say?
Do I know the intent behind the practices I keep, or only the practices?
What in my life needs pricking continually rather than deciding once?
